title: Rodi v. Southern New England School of Law
lead: A student alleged that accreditation assurances kept him at an unaccredited law school. After discovery, his fraud claims failed on actual and reasonable reliance despite an earlier victory at the pleading stage.

actors.name: Joseph Rodi
actors.role: Law student seeking eventual New Jersey bar eligibility

actors.name: Southern New England School of Law
Francis Larkin and David Prentiss
actors.role: Successive deans whose statements formed the pleaded fraud claim

actors.name: Judge Howard
actors.role: Author of the unanimous First Circuit opinion

proceedings: An initial New Jersey suit was dismissed for lack of personal jurisdiction; Massachusetts litigation followed.
A 2004 appeal partly reversed pleading-stage dismissal; discovery then led to summary judgment.
The 2008 First Circuit affirmed substantive judgment and retention by the original judge; recusal argument was waived.
limits: The 2008 appeal assumed possible knowing material falsehoods and inducement, resolving reliance instead.
Accreditation and bar-admission rules described here are historical; no current status is asserted.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Rodi enrolls with accreditation still uncertain
sections.cue: Introduce the school and the goal driving enrollment.
paragraphs: Joseph Rodi applied to Southern New England School of Law in March 1997 knowing it lacked American Bar Association accreditation. The Association’s Accreditation Committee had recommended provisional approval, but two other Association bodies still had to approve. Dean Francis Larkin told prospective students he was highly confident of favorable decisions in August. Rodi enrolled hoping eventually to take New Jersey’s bar examination, which required an accredited-school degree. Provisional approval would provide the necessary recognition; full approval required at least two years of provisional status.

In August, the Association denied provisional approval for substantial noncompliance and other concerns. At a September student meeting, Larkin said the school had corrected its deficiencies and promised approval on the next application before students graduated. The catalogue, however, disclaimed any representation that approval would occur before a particular student’s graduation.

sections.title: Transfer applications continue despite renewed optimism
sections.cue: Trace the events through graduation and litigation.
paragraphs: After his first year, in summer 1998, Rodi applied to transfer to Rutgers and Seton Hall. New acting dean David Prentiss asked him to reconsider and expressed optimism about ultimate accreditation. Rodi withdrew neither application; both schools rejected him. Discovery later showed that Larkin privately lacked high confidence after the first rejection, and Prentiss recognized limited school resources and did not know how the Association would rule. Those facts were viewed favorably to Rodi on summary judgment, not determined by a trial verdict.

In November 1999, the Accreditation Committee rejected the renewed application for continuing noncompliance and lack of a reliable three-year compliance plan. The school did not appeal. Rodi graduated in September 2000 without the accreditation necessary for his New Jersey objective.

His July 2002 New Jersey federal suit was dismissed for lack of personal jurisdiction. In June 2003, he sued the school and both deans in Massachusetts, alleging fraud and violation of Massachusetts Chapter 93A. A 2004 First Circuit decision partly reversed dismissal and allowed proceedings to continue. The original district judge retained the remanded case over a reassignment motion. After discovery, the judge assumed potentially false material statements but entered summary judgment because reliance was unreasonable.

sections.title: The evidence does not support the claimed reliance
sections.cue: Explain why the earlier pleading ruling did not settle this appeal.
paragraphs: In the 2008 appeal, Judge Howard wrote for Judges Torruella, Lipez and himself. Reviewing de novo under Massachusetts law, the court required a knowing material falsehood intended to induce action, detrimental actual reliance, and reasonable reliance. Reasonableness ordinarily belonged to a jury, but not when no reasonable jury could find it. The earlier pleading-stage ruling did not establish that the developed evidence met those requirements.

Rodi alleged that the deans knowingly reassured him to prevent student departures and caused him to forgo alternatives, including a doctorate. He claimed tuition, lost earnings during attendance, and possible doctoral financial benefits. The court assumed the disputed falsehood and inducement premises, without awarding those alleged losses.

His continued transfer efforts contradicted his unexplained assertion that belief in the deans kept him at the school. Transfer applications were not inherently incompatible with reliance: he might have preferred studying nearer home or found withdrawal inconvenient. But he supplied no such explanation in evidence. A conclusory reliance assertion could not reconcile the record. The proposed doctorate likewise lacked persuasive support when the assurances had not even induced withdrawal of pending transfer applications. No reasonable jury could find actual reliance.

sections.title: The content and context also defeat reasonable reliance
sections.cue: Identify the warnings without making disclaimers absolute.
paragraphs: Only Larkin’s September 1997 statement and Prentiss’s July 1998 letter were pleaded with sufficient particularity. General student affidavits about numerous assurances did not identify the necessary speaker, content, place and time. Other administrators’ statements lacked developed arguments on knowing inducement and reasonable reliance. Larkin’s promise to reapply was not analyzed as deception because the school did reapply.

The claim that substantial deficiencies had been fixed in four weeks was implausible in context. Larkin’s promised approval before graduation also faced the catalogue disclaimer, the Association’s independent authority, and his failed forecast of August approval. The court expressly refused to make disclaimers automatic fraud defenses; this disclaimer was one contextual warning. Students had already watched the independent accreditor reject the school’s optimism. Failure to obtain approval before the then-third-year students graduated gave another warning under the alleged student-body-wide assurance.

Prentiss’s letter was weaker still: it predicted ultimate approval, not approval before Rodi graduated, as the time available to finish at an accredited school dwindled. Trust in the deans could not overcome their actual words and circumstances. Any reliance would therefore also have been unreasonable.

sections.title: The statutory and judicial-assignment challenges also fail
sections.cue: End with each issue’s distinct disposition.
paragraphs: Chapter 93A prohibited unfair or deceptive trade or commerce practices. Rodi’s particular theory rested on fraudulent misrepresentation and required reasonable reliance, so that claim failed too. The court did not hold that every Chapter 93A theory requires common-law fraud. It reached the merits without deciding the school’s separate thirty-day demand-letter objection.

Rodi also argued on appeal that the district judge’s graduation speech, honorary degree and favorable accreditation comments required recusal. He had not requested recusal below; his reassignment motion had relied only on saving time. The recusal argument was waived, not rejected on a finding that such connections could never matter.

Reassignment was preserved. Local Rule 40.1(K)(2) allowed retention on remand when required by the remand or when substantial time savings and the interests of justice supported it. Applying abuse-of-discretion review, the court upheld retention because the judge knew the background and procedural history and had held a status conference. The earlier absence of an answer or completed discovery did not negate those savings.
On June 30, 2008, the First Circuit affirmed in full, without damages, new trial or reassignment. No separate opinion was reported.
